title: About
text:
An emaki (絵巻) is a Japanese picture handscroll: a long painted scene held between two rolls of paper, read by winding it from one to the other, a span at a time. It is a good name for a window whose job is a conversation too long to see at once.
The app’s icon is a handscroll seen from the front, with a conversation on its sheet — the agent on the left with its spark, your reply on the right. The drawing on the home page is the same scroll, with a landscape on it, and it winds as you move across it.

text:

The app’s icon is a handscroll seen from the front, with a conversation on its sheet — the agent on the left with its spark, your reply on the right. The drawing on the home page is the same scroll, with a landscape on it, and it winds as you move across it.

title: About
text:
Why it exists
Claude Code deletes its transcripts after cleanupPeriodDays, thirty by default, with no warning. Every other tool in this space reads ~/.claude/projects and stops there, so they all inherit that expiry.
So Emaki copies first and renders second. The archive sweep runs before anything else touches a session, for exactly this reason: if rendering fails, the bytes are already safe. The archive is not a backup but a peer source — live and archived transcripts are unioned, so a session Claude Code has deleted stays listed, searchable, renderable and exportable, flagged as kept.
Compaction, for what it is worth, was never the threat: it appends a boundary and keeps writing to the same file, leaving the earlier rows intact.

title: About
text:
How it is built
Rust, with GPUI — the Zed editor’s UI framework — and gpui-component for the window. There is no daemon, no browser and no hook.
crates/emaki-core    everything without a window, plus the emaki-core CLI
crates/emaki-app     the window
vendor/              the gpui-component crates, with a few changes of ours
scripts/             packaging, the icon, the status line
The core works in this order:

Adapters, one per agent, find each agent’s sessions on disk.
Archive copies them byte for byte, before anything else touches them.
Build parses the JSONL transcript into a model of rounds, items and tool calls. The transcript is the only source of truth.
Render writes that model as markdown under ~/.emaki/logs.
Search indexes every item in SQLite FTS5.

The app reads the same model and draws it. A file watcher says when to look again. To reply, it either writes to a terminal session’s inbox socket or runs a headless claude -p --resume child that appends to the same transcript.

title: About
text:
Where it is going
Three stages. The first is a complete app for Claude Code — permanent history, organization by recency, project and agent, readable conversations, and an explanation on any step. The second is the public release and the feedback that comes with it. The third extends the same features to Codex, Kimi and the other mainstream coding agents, so Emaki works across all of them.
Codex support landed in v0.2.0; the releases are the honest record of where things actually are.

title: About
text:
Credits
The home page’s figure follows the line-drawing manner of hairline’s figures: nothing filled, no words, what is far is dimmer, and one bright mark.
Icons are Tabler’s outline set, drawn at a stroke of 1.75 where Tabler’s own is 2. The file tree’s icons are Catppuccin’s. The code colours are Rosé Pine’s hues, retinted for contrast. The terminal keeps Kaku’s cream in the light appearance. Every face the app carries is under the SIL Open Font License.

title: Emaki
text:
Every coding-agent session on your machine, kept for good, in one window you can also talk to.


An agentic development environment: not an editor that an agent was added to, but a window built around the sessions themselves.


Download What’s in it Source

title: Emaki
text:
The thirty-day problem
Claude Code deletes its transcripts after thirty days, with no warning. Every other tool in this space reads ~/.claude/projects and stops there, so they all inherit that expiry.
Emaki copies every Claude Code and Codex session before that happens, renders and searches all of them, and lets you continue a Claude Code session from the window. It never writes to a transcript and adds nothing to a session’s context.


Kept for good
Every session is copied byte for byte into ~/.emaki/archive before anything else touches it. One that Claude Code has since deleted is still there, still listed, still searchable, marked kept.


Search everything
⌘K searches every session you have ever run, indexed a paragraph at a time. ⌘F finds inside the one you are reading.


Read what it did
Prompts, replies, thoughts, tool calls and subagents, laid out like the Claude app rather than scrolled past in a terminal. Every session also renders to a markdown file.


Carry on talking
Type in the composer to reply. A session running in a terminal gets the message through Claude Code’s inbox; a finished one resumes under Emaki.

title: Emaki
section: Nothing it will do to you
text:
Nothing it will do to you
No hooks, ever. Nothing writes to a transcript, and nothing Emaki does enters a session’s context window. It types in no terminal of yours and asks no terminal app for anything — it runs its own, hidden. There is no daemon and no browser.
Everything lives in ~/.emaki. Only archive/ cannot be rebuilt, so that is the one directory to back up.

title: Emaki
section: Built on the agents you already use
text:
Built on the agents you already use
Emaki needs Claude Code or Codex installed; it adds three things on top of them. Conversations that never expire, one place to organize them, and a readable view of what the agent did.

Install Emaki

title: Features
text: Most of Emaki explains itself once it is open. This is the tour, and the shortcuts are at the foot.

title: Features
text:
Sessions and projects
The sidebar lists every project, with pinned ones above the rest and headings at the foot for hidden projects and temporary folders. All Sessions unfolds each project in place, every session dated, archived projects in their own section.
Select sessions or projects together — ⌘-click, ⇧-click, a dragged rectangle, or ⌘A — then archive them now, delete them, or open them in Finder. Archive checks Emaki’s own copy first; Delete moves every copy to the Trash. Nothing in a project’s own folder is touched.
A session Claude Code has deleted stays listed, marked kept. Renaming a session renames it for Claude Code too. Each one keeps its own draft.
Tabs group into per-project pills, drag to reorder, and answer to ⌘1–⌘9.

title: Features
text:
Search
⌘K searches every session on the machine. The index holds one document per item — a prompt, a reply paragraph, a thought, a tool call — so a hit lands on the thing you remembered rather than the file it was in. Live and archived sessions are searched together.
⌘F finds inside the conversation you are reading, ⌘G and ⌘⇧G step through the hits.

title: Features
text:
Conversation
Prompts, replies, tool calls, thoughts and subagents, laid out like the Claude app. Prompts sit in a bubble with a tail; tool badges are coloured by kind; tool calls, thoughts and rows open and close in motion rather than jumping. Code blocks are syntax-coloured, carry a copy button, and scroll sideways instead of wrapping.
Explain puts one plain sentence on an opaque tool call, asked of the session’s own agent — Haiku for Claude Code, Codex’s light model for Codex.
The outline (⌘⇧O) is a short label per prompt; click one to jump there. A progress note shows as part of the reply, as it does in the terminal, and a running command says what it is for.

title: Features
text:
Composer
Type to reply. A session running in a terminal gets the message through Claude Code’s inbox; a finished one resumes under Emaki.

Attach files by paste, drop, or the + button.
@ picks a file or folder from the project. An existing path takes the accent colour.
/ lists the folder’s slash commands.
Spelling and grammar are checked as you type (English US and UK; Spanish, French and German spelling on a Mac), with corrections, Learn Spelling and Ignore on the right-click menu.
Dictation (⌘⇧D) writes down what you say, on this machine, with a model you download in Settings — Qwen3-ASR or Whisper, Chinese and English mixed. macOS for now.
Send with ⌘↩︎ or ↩︎, your choice; ⇧↩︎ is always a new line. Drafts survive quitting.

title: Features
text:
Agent control
Mode, model and effort are pills under the composer, each in the agent’s own colours, each opening a list in place. ⇧Tab steps the mode as it does in the terminal. Approvals, questions and plans arrive as cards — including whatever the agent asks that Emaki has no card for, so nothing waits unseen. A plan is shown on its approval card and kept in the conversation.
Stop a turn from the window, and the stopped message comes back to the composer if the agent had not started on it.
The row under the composer shows context left and rate limits, for both agents.

title: Features
text:
Terminal
The button at the top right opens a terminal beside the conversation: a shell in the session’s folder, or the session’s own agent as it runs, drawn whole and two-way. Shells open in tabs. Mouse selection copies on release, mouse-aware programs take clicks and scrolls, and the Mac’s terminal line keys work (⌘←, ⌘→, ⌘⌫, ⇧↩︎, ⌘K).
⌘⇧S and ⌘⇧A show and hide the two sides of the panel.

title: Features
text:
Files and editing
The files panel is a tree of the project with git’s marks on it, and it works like a file manager: drag in from Finder, drag rows to move, cut, copy, duplicate, remove with ⌘⌫, undo with ⌘Z.
Click a file to open it in a pane beside the conversation:







Code
line numbers, colours, a gutter mark per git change with a card to see or revert it


Markdown
as it reads or as written; a YAML header shows as a table of its fields


CSV
a grid with lettered columns, editable in place, each column its own colour


Parquet
a table with each column’s type and the row count


Word
pages you can type in, style and format, saved with ⌘S


PowerPoint, Excel
slides drawn as they look, cells with their number formats


PDF
sharp at any width, with search, selection, page previews and a table of contents


HTML
in the system’s web view, scripts and all


Pictures
shown



Unsaved changes are never lost without asking. Format on save covers ten languages — R, Python, Rust, Go, C and C++, TypeScript, JavaScript, JSON, Markdown, TOML — and is off until you turn it on.

title: Features
text:
Git
The Changes sheet commits the files you tick, discards several at once, and has a History tab: browse commits, undo the last one, revert one. Push, Pull and Fetch sit where the counts are. Branches can be listed, created, switched (carrying changes along or leaving them behind) and published.

title: Features
text:
Settings
⌘, opens nine pages: Appearance, Fonts, Composer, Dictate, New sessions, Terminal, Files, Updates, About.
Appearance follows the system or pins light or dark, and the accent is one of six — terracotta, blue, green, violet, teal, graphite. Eight chat faces and four monospace faces ship with the app, all under the Open Font License, with one text size across the conversation, the file editor and the terminal.

title: Features
text:
What it will not do
These hold everywhere, by design:

No hooks, ever.
Nothing writes to a transcript. The JSONL file is the only source of truth, and Emaki is a reader of it.
Nothing Emaki does enters a session’s context window.
Nothing is typed into a terminal of yours, and no terminal app is asked for anything. Emaki runs its own, hidden.
Copy first, render second. If rendering fails, the bytes are already safe.

Esc

title: Releases
text: Every release, newest first. The installers are on the releases page; the app also updates itself from Settings.

title: Releases
text:
v0.2.6 · 15 October 2026

Dictation post-processing: a small model downloaded to this Mac (Qwen3.5 4B, 2B or 0.8B) removes hesitations, applies corrections (“100, no, 200”), mends grammar and makes lists, in any language, without translating. Turn it on in Settings, Dictate.
Settings, Dictate has two lists, Speech to Text and Post-processing, each showing the model in use and opening to the rest. Several models can download at once.
Dictation history: kept on this Mac for as long as you choose, with a window to look back and copy what was said, as heard or post-processed.
Dictation starts and stops on a modifier tapped alone, such as Right ⌘ or Fn, chosen under More; Esc cancels it while listening. Softer chimes.
The Agents page shows the steps for this machine only, and GitHub in place of GitHub Desktop.
Every button has an icon, and every Off and On switch turns at a click anywhere on it.
Fixes: sessions ordered by when they last did something; a tooltip left on screen after its sheet closed; text that went on selecting after a click in the Changes sheet; scrolling in a window over Settings.

title: Releases
text:

Settings has a page a section, Off and On for every switch, a field for dictation’s key with Reset, and an About page.
Codex sessions are archived, unarchived and deleted through Codex itself, and an archived session is unarchived from its menu in the sidebar.
The Agents page walks through installing git and each agent and signing in, a numbered step at a time, for the system you choose.
Cards that come up while a session runs stand at the conversation’s end and scroll with it; a dialog’s tabs sit in a strip with arrows.

title: Releases

Word documents open as pages and can be written in: type, select, style, format, undo and save with ⌘S, on WordCraft’s engine. Try it on a copy first: a save rewrites the file.
PowerPoint slides are drawn as they look, Excel cells show their number formats, and PDF pages are sharp at any width.

title: Releases
text:

A new look: the sidebar and a thin frame around the content in graphite, the page near white, and in the dark appearance a darker page in a lighter frame.
Settings, Fonts: eight chat fonts and four monospace fonts, all built into the app, and one font size for the conversation, the file editor and the terminal.
Format on save covers ten languages: R, Python, Rust, Go, C and C++, TypeScript, JavaScript, JSON, Markdown and TOML. It is off until you turn it on.

/clear is followed to the session it starts.

title: Releases
text:
v0.2.0 · 10 October 2026

Codex joins Claude Code: its sessions are kept, read and searched, and you can start, continue and stop one from the window, with its approvals, questions and plans on the same cards.
Codex’s own terminal is on the terminal panel, joined to the same session, so a turn typed there shows in the conversation and the other way round.
An Agents page (⌘E) says which agents are installed and signed in, with the commands to set one up and a shell beside them.
A new session’s agent is chosen on the strip under the composer, also on one begun from a project’s plus. Its mode, effort and model are lists there, and Settings, New sessions has them for each agent.
The mode pill opens a list for Claude Code too, in each mode’s colour; ⇧Tab still steps as in the terminal.
The row under the composer shows context and usage for Codex, with whatever windows its plan has.
Each agent has its colour: Claude’s terracotta and Codex’s green, on its mark and on its page.
Tabs keep a readable width and scroll once they no longer fit, the tab you are on stays in view, and ⌘ shows 1 to 9 on the tabs those keys go to.
Branches: fetch, make a branch from the list, publish a local one, and see how to sign in when the remote refuses.
A plan is shown on its approval card and stays in the conversation, and tool calls, thoughts and rows open and close in motion.
The archive is a folder an agent; an older one is moved into place at launch.
Fixes: a session begun from a folder no longer ends with “No conversation found”, and lists in the dark appearance show the row under the pointer.

title: Releases
text:

Edit files in the pane beside the conversation and save with ⌘S. Unsaved changes are never lost without asking, and git’s changes are marked in the margin, each with a card to see or revert it.

Word, PowerPoint and Excel files (docx, pptx, xlsx, xls) open to read.

title: Releases

Open in your terminal: continue a session with claude --resume in a terminal window.
A session opens at its end and follows the reply as it streams.
Text matches the Claude app: 16px, semibold for bold, monospaced inline code.
Claude’s own mark, turning while it works.
Notices show under the composer, not in the sidebar.
Fixed: bold drew as regular, scroll momentum crossed panes, arrow keys stopped short of the composer’s ends.

title: Releases
text:
v0.1.1 · 29 September 2026
The app stands alone. The Python command-line tool and web daemon are gone.

Emaki updates itself, from Settings or a daily check.
Explain: one plain sentence on what an opaque tool call does, on tool cards and permission cards.
Context and rate limits under the composer.
Long tool output scrolls inside its card.
Pasted pictures show their names.
Fixed: a crash on some Codex sessions, and ⌘↩︎ leaving a line break.
No hooks. If ~/.claude/settings.json still has entries naming emaki-hook, delete them.

title: Releases
text:
v0.1.0 · 29 September 2026
The first release. Emaki keeps every coding-agent session on your machine and lets you read, search and continue them in one window.

Every Claude Code and Codex session is archived byte for byte, and stays after Claude Code deletes it.
A board of live sessions: needs you, planning, working, your turn.
Full-text search across every session (⌘K), and find inside one (⌘F).
A conversation view laid out like the Claude app.
Reply from the window, with attachments, permission cards, and mode, model and effort pills.
Every session also renders to a markdown file.
Settings for appearance, accent, font and text size.

Install: on macOS drag Emaki to Applications (signed and notarized). On Windows SmartScreen asks once: More info, then Run anyway. On Linux run the AppImage or install the .deb.

title: Install
text:
Download the installer for your system. Each link takes the asset from the latest release.
The Mac downloads are disk images, Windows an installer, Linux an AppImage. A .deb is on the release page too.
macOS 14 or later. The Mac image is signed and notarized, so it opens without argument. Windows is unsigned, so SmartScreen asks once: More info, then Run anyway.

title: Install
text:
You need an agent first
Emaki reads and drives the coding agents already on your machine, so at least one of them has to be installed and signed in:

Claude Code — fully supported: read, search, and continue a session from the window.
Codex — read, search, start, continue and stop, with approvals, questions and plans on the same cards.

The Agents page in the app (⌘E) shows which are installed and which are signed in, and walks through installing git and each agent a numbered step at a time for your system, with a shell beside the instructions.

title: Install
text:
The first launch
Open the app. The first launch copies every transcript it finds into ~/.emaki/archive, and every later launch catches up. Capture does not depend on the app running: whenever you open it, it backfills every session you have ever run.
Everything Emaki keeps is under ~/.emaki:







archive/
every session, copied byte for byte, one folder per agent


logs/
each session rendered as markdown


search.db
the full-text index


config.json
your settings



Only archive/ cannot be rebuilt from something else. That is the directory to back up.

title: Install
text:
The one thing it changes
Emaki sets a single thing in Claude Code’s settings: its own status line, which feeds the context and rate-limit row shown under the composer. Nothing else is touched, and no hook is installed.
To put your old status line back:
emaki-core statusline restore

title: Install
text:
Updating
The app updates itself — from Settings, or on a daily check. Nothing to reinstall.

title: Install
text:
Building from source
Rust, with GPUI:
git clone https://github.com/alkaline-software/emaki
cd emaki
cargo build -p emaki-app && ./target/debug/Emaki
On a Mac the build needs CMake (brew install cmake) for the dictation model runner.
